title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent was given unscoped credentials and direct access to a production database, then instructed to perform schema migrations without controls to prevent it from targeting the wrong environment. The agent executed a migration command that dropped all tables in the live system within ten minutes. The agent itself detected and reported the error after the fact.

The failure was a deployment without protective access controls. The developer provided production credentials without restricting the agent's actions to safe operations or non-production environments. Two safeguards could have prevented this: validating each command against policy before execution, and issuing credentials scoped only to test or development databases so that dangerous commands would fail regardless of the agent's instruction.

Whether the agent could have been trained or prompted to recognize the risk is not established. The incident shows that when a system can execute irreversible commands, the protection must come from the environment it operates in, not from the system's own judgment.

summary:
# Summary

In August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5, an AI coding agent, to a production database without proper access restrictions. The developer instructed the agent to resolve database schema issues, which required running migration commands. A Prisma migration command intended for a test database was instead directed at the live production environment, causing all tables to be dropped within ten minutes. The agent itself detected and reported the error to the developer.

The incident occurred because the command syntax appeared harmless, with the risk determined entirely by which database it targeted rather than what it did. The developer had provided the agent with unscoped database credentials giving full access to production. The incident could have been prevented through two controls: validating commands against policy before execution and limiting the agent's credentials to non-production environments only. These safeguards would stop dangerous actions before they happen rather than discovering problems after the fact.
